title: IMMUNODEFICIENCY 35
alt_titles: HYPER-IgE SYNDROME WITH ATYPICAL MYCOBACTERIOSIS, AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE
HIES WITH ATYPICAL MYCOBACTERIOSIS, AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that immunodeficiency-35 (IMD35) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the TYK2 gene (176941) on chromosome 19p13.

checks.claim: Immunodeficiency-35 (IMD35) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the TYK2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: (a) TYK2 gene mutation; (b) Autosomal recessive inheritance;
checks.explanation: Paper reports a homozygous TYK2 mutation in its patient and lists compound heterozygous TYK2 mutations in P10/P11 (Nemoto) in Table 3; disease name IMD35 is nomenclature.

checks.claim: The TYK2 gene is located on chromosome 19p13.
checks.evidence_quote: Tyrosine kinase 2 (Tyk2) is a nonreceptor tyrosine kinase that belongs to the Janus kinase (Jak) family.
checks.explanation: The chromosomal location is standard nomenclature for the gene the paper studies.

paragraphs.text: Immunodeficiency-35 (IMD35) is an autosomal recessive primary immunodeficiency caused by tyrosine kinase-2 (TYK2) deficiency. Affected people are susceptible to intracellular bacteria, mainly mycobacteria (including BCG and environmental mycobacteria) and Salmonella, and to viral infections. The first reported patient also had features of hyper-IgE syndrome, including atopic dermatitis and very high serum IgE. Patients reported later did not have hyper-IgE syndrome. The cellular defect is impaired response to IL-12 and type I interferons (IFN-alpha/beta), which require TYK2 for signaling.

paragraphs.text: The disorder was first described as an autosomal recessive form of hyper-IgE syndrome with atypical mycobacteriosis (Minegishi et al., 2006). Later reports showed that hyper-IgE syndrome is not a constant feature of TYK2 deficiency (Kreins et al., 2015).

checks.evidence_quote: Here we identified a homozygous Tyk2 mutation in a patient who had been clinically diagnosed with hyper-IgE syndrome. This patient showed unusual susceptibility to various microorganisms including virus, fungi, and mycobacteria
checks.explanation: Hyper-IgE syndrome, a homozygous mutation and mycobacterial susceptibility are reported. The abstract does not use the phrases 'autosomal recessive form' or 'atypical mycobacteriosis'.

checks.claim: Hyper-IgE syndrome is not a constant feature of TYK2 deficiency.
checks.evidence_quote: Moreover, impaired IL-6 responses and HIES do not appear to be intrinsic features of TYK2 deficiency in humans.
checks.explanation: Stated in conclusion.

paragraphs.text: Minegishi et al. (2006) reported a Japanese patient with features of hyper-IgE syndrome: atopic dermatitis and highly elevated serum IgE. He also had unusual susceptibility to intracellular pathogens, including mycobacteria (BCG), Salmonella, and herpes simplex virus, as well as staphylococcal skin infections.

paragraphs.text: Kreins et al. (2015) reported further TYK2-deficient patients from several families of different ethnic origins. They had mycobacterial infections (BCG and/or tuberculosis) and/or viral infections. None had hyper-IgE syndrome or markedly elevated IgE. The authors concluded that hyper-IgE syndrome is not a consistent feature of TYK2 deficiency.

paragraphs.text: The transmission pattern of IMD35 is autosomal recessive. Minegishi et al. (2006) and Kreins et al. (2015) found biallelic TYK2 mutations in affected individuals.

checks.evidence_quote: Thus, the seven patients from five kindreds reported here probably had autosomal recessive (AR) TYK2 deficiency
checks.explanation: AR stated.

checks.evidence_quote: Here we identified a homozygous Tyk2 mutation in a patient
checks.explanation: A homozygous mutation is a biallelic mutation.

checks.claim: Kreins et al. (2015) found biallelic TYK2 mutations in individuals affected with IMD35.
checks.evidence_quote: We identified homozygous mutations in TYK2 by linkage analysis and Sanger sequencing (P2), WES (P3 to P7), or targeted NGS (P8).
checks.explanation: Homozygous mutations are biallelic.

paragraphs.text: In a Japanese patient with hyper-IgE syndrome and atypical mycobacteriosis, Minegishi et al. (2006) found a homozygous 4-bp deletion in the TYK2 gene. The deletion caused a frameshift and premature termination, and TYK2 protein was absent. The patient's cells had defective signaling in response to several cytokines, including type I interferons, IL-6, IL-10, IL-12, and IL-23. This was accompanied by skewing toward Th2 differentiation, which may explain the high IgE and atopy.

checks.claim: Minegishi et al. (2006) found a homozygous 4-bp deletion in the TYK2 gene in a Japanese patient with hyper-IgE syndrome and atypical mycobacteriosis.
checks.evidence_quote: Here we identified a homozygous Tyk2 mutation in a patient who had been clinically diagnosed with hyper-IgE syndrome.
checks.explanation: A homozygous mutation in a patient with hyper-IgE syndrome is reported. The abstract does not describe the 4-bp deletion, Japanese origin or atypical mycobacteriosis.

checks.explanation: The abstract does not say the TYK2 protein was absent.

checks.explanation: All five cytokines named in the claim are listed in the abstract.

checks.evidence_quote: including the phenotype of impaired T helper 1 (Th1) differentiation and accelerated Th2 differentiation
checks.explanation: Accelerated Th2 differentiation is stated.

checks.explanation: The abstract links Th2 skewing to the clinical picture, but it does not explicitly say Th2 skewing explains the high IgE and atopy.

paragraphs.text: Kreins et al. (2015) found homozygous TYK2 mutations in further patients. Most of the mutations caused complete loss of TYK2 expression. The patients' cells had impaired responses to IL-12 and IFN-alpha/beta, leading to reduced IFN-gamma production. However, responses to IL-6, IL-10, and IL-23 were largely preserved. This contrasted with the findings in the first patient and fits the lack of hyper-IgE syndrome in these patients.

checks.claim: Kreins et al. (2015) found homozygous TYK2 mutations in further patients with TYK2 deficiency.
checks.evidence_quote: These patients were homozygous for one of five null mutations, different from that seen in P1.
checks.explanation: Stated.

checks.claim: Most of the TYK2 mutations reported by Kreins et al. (2015) caused complete loss of TYK2 expression.
checks.evidence_quote: The 130-kD TYK2 protein, which was detectable in control cells, was undetectable in cells from all patients
checks.explanation: Paper reports loss of TYK2 expression in all patients, not 'most'.

checks.claim: Cells from the TYK2-deficient patients reported by Kreins et al. (2015) had impaired responses to IL-12 and IFN-alpha/beta.
checks.evidence_quote: All eight TYK2-deficient patients displayed impaired but not abolished cellular responses to (a) IL-12 and IFN-α/β
checks.explanation: Stated.

checks.claim: Impaired IL-12 response in cells from the TYK2-deficient patients reported by Kreins et al. (2015) led to reduced IFN-gamma production.
checks.evidence_quote: whole blood from P2, P3, P4, P5, P6, and P7 displayed impaired but not abolished IFN-γ induction after stimulation with BCG plus IL-12 for 48 h
checks.explanation: Reduced IFN-γ production shown.

checks.claim: Responses to IL-6, IL-10, and IL-23 were largely preserved in cells from the TYK2-deficient patients reported by Kreins et al. (2015).
checks.explanation: Only IL-6 responses were normal; IL-23 and IL-10 responses were impaired: 'All eight TYK2-deficient patients displayed impaired but not abolished cellular responses to ... (b) IL-23 ... and (c) IL-10'.

checks.claim: The preserved IL-6, IL-10, and IL-23 responses in the patients reported by Kreins et al. (2015) contrasted with the findings in the first TYK2-deficient patient.
checks.explanation: Only IL-6 differed from P1; 'given that the response to the cytokines IFN-α, IL-12, IL-23, and IL-10 are equally impaired in all TYK2-deficient patients (including P1)'.

checks.claim: The preserved IL-6, IL-10, and IL-23 responses fit the lack of hyper-IgE syndrome in the TYK2-deficient patients reported by Kreins et al. (2015).
checks.explanation: Paper attributes lack of HIES to normal IL-6 responses only; IL-10 and IL-23 were impaired and 'defects in these responses are unlikely to be the cause of HIES in P1'.

paragraphs.text: Boisson-Dupuis et al. (2018) found that homozygosity for the common TYK2 variant P1104A is a cause of mycobacterial disease, including tuberculosis. This variant selectively impairs IL-23 signaling but leaves IL-12 and IFN-alpha/beta responses largely intact. Kerner et al. (2019) found an association between P1104A homozygosity and tuberculosis in a large population cohort.

checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 8 cited papers. This claim concerns a later study (Boisson-Dupuis 2018) that this paper does not address.

checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 8 cited papers. This claim concerns Kerner et al. (2019), which this paper does not address.

paragraphs.text: Boisson-Dupuis et al. (2018) found that homozygosity for the common TYK2 variant pro1104-to-ala (P1104A) confers susceptibility to mycobacterial disease, including tuberculosis. The variant protein is catalytically impaired. It selectively disrupts IL-23-dependent induction of IFN-gamma but leaves responses to IL-12 and type I interferons largely intact. Kerner et al. (2019) found that P1104A homozygosity was associated with tuberculosis in a large population cohort.
